name: Ideal Parent Figure Protocol
origin: Developed in the United States over about two decades by psychologists Daniel Brown of Harvard Medical School and David Elliott with collaborators, and set out in their 2016 book Attachment Disturbances in Adults: Treatment for Comprehensive Repair (Norton).
summary: The Ideal Parent Figure Protocol is a guided imagery method for adults with insecure attachment, meaning lasting patterns of anxiety, avoidance or confusion in close relationships that attachment research links to early care. With a therapist's guidance, the client imagines being a child with a new set of parents, not the ones they grew up with, who show five qualities linked to secure attachment: they protect, soothe, tune in to the child's feelings, encourage exploration and growth, and openly delight in the child. It is one of three pillars in Brown and Elliott's treatment, alongside work on reflecting about one's own and other people's minds and on building cooperation in relationships.
theoryOfChange: Attachment theory holds that early experiences with caregivers become inner models of oneself and others that later shape whether a person feels worthy of care and safe with others. Studies show that imagining a responsive, caring figure can bring a brief feeling of security, and the method aims to make that change last by vividly and repeatedly experiencing the kinds of care that build secure attachment. Over time this is thought to build new inner models and support earned security, a shift toward secure attachment in adulthood.
whatYouDo: After a short guided body-scan relaxation, the therapist guides the client to vividly imagine being a child with ideal parent figures, who can be wholly invented or loosely based on real or fictional people with the right qualities. The therapist describes how these parents meet the child's needs, for example comforting the child when overwhelmed, and the client is encouraged to feel the experience in the body while the therapist helps them keep imagination separate from memories of their own childhood. The developers advise tailoring the imagery to each client's attachment needs (the 2017 pilot instead used five standard scenes), and the practice is repeated across sessions, sometimes with a recording for home use.
typicalDose: Usually part of ongoing individual therapy, which the developers describe as longer-term work lasting from several months to several years. In the 2017 pilot it was given as four weekly sessions, each with about 16 minutes of guided imagery, plus a recording for practice at home.
keyTechniques: Imagining being a child with ideal parents
Parents who protect, soothe, attune, encourage and delight
Feeling the imagined care in the body
Repeating the practice, including with a home recording

evidence.summary: The first independent test was a 2017 open pilot at a public clinic in France, in which 17 adults with complex PTSD from childhood trauma had four weekly sessions using one standard imagery script of about 16 minutes plus a recording for home practice. Overall symptoms and markers of attachment trauma fell and quality of life rose with medium to large effects, and the 13 people reassessed about eight months later had kept their gains on the three questionnaires, though dissociative and bodily symptoms did not change. With no control group, the study could not rule out placebo effects, natural swings in symptoms or the effect of the therapy relationship. The developers' book also reports that all 12 clients in their own long-term therapy pilot (about 3.4 years on average) ended with an earned secure attachment rating, but that study was small and run by the developers themselves, and no randomized controlled trials were found.

goodFitFor: Adults who feel anxious about being left, uneasy with closeness, or confused about trust in close relationships and want to work on the early roots of that with a trained therapist. It has also been tested as an early, stabilizing step for adults with complex trauma from childhood, and because it relies on imagery and felt experience it may suit people who are comfortable working that way.
cautions: Imagining being cared for may bring painful memories of one's real childhood to the surface; in the 2017 pilot one person's attachment rating worsened, which the authors linked to buried trauma emerging, so it is best done with a therapist trained in both the method and trauma care. Given the thin evidence, it should not replace well-tested treatments for PTSD, depression or other conditions without professional advice.
namingNote: IPF here means the Ideal Parent Figure Protocol, not interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) and not idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a lung disease with the same abbreviation. This entry covers the imagery protocol; the wider Three Pillars treatment in Brown and Elliott's book also includes metacognitive work (reflecting on minds) and collaborative work (cooperation in relationships). David Elliott continues to teach the method, now within a broader approach called Integrative Attachment Therapy.
